534/Lectures/Week-1---Narrative-Roles.content:
Summary: Video games use image, sound, and text to communicate. This session sets up the cinematic vocabulary we will use all semester, then introduces four narrative roles — The Investigator, The Traveler, The Entrant, and The Dreamer — that organize your first three projects.










Course Overview



A Note on Terms
First!
This presentation refers to the creator as the “designer” or “filmmaker” and so on.
The audience and players will be referred to as “us” and “we”. And “our”.










Cinematic Language
Video games use image, sound, and text to communicate
This class will prioritize analyzing cinematic language.
We will study and practice every week.











Deep versus shallow focus on the same subject.
For example
Depth of field shapes our attention and our take on subjectivity.











The color wheel.
So does the use of color.











The Favourite (2018) - an extreme wide-angle lens distorts the room and the power in it.
Game engine cameras mimic the terms and features of physical ones, and cinematography broadly.
(Focal length, f-stops, lens filters, focus, light types, and so on).










So that (for example)
Creators can practice “show don’t tell”.
(And be savvy at breaking any such rules that they have mastered).











Shadow of the Colossus (2005).
With such grammar in hand, a visual storyteller can craft a character’s point-of-view.










Artists and designers want to communicate in order to question and persuade.
Two of the class’s primary themes are the player’s experiences of control and discovery.
Let’s get into that…










Narrative Roles
Your first three assignments are framed by a sequence of narrative roles.
Player’s experiences are shaped by the role they are given – what the player can and does do.
This class will study four such roles with pragmatism:
three provide constraints for assignments during our first 10 weeks, while The Entrant clarifies the transition from discovery to control.










The Protagonist

Horizon Zero Dawn (2017).
First, What is a main character?
The most common cinematic storytelling framework centers around the protagonist, the pursuit of most professional storytellers from all mediums.











Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (1983).
The Protagonist

Get Out (2017).
The Protagonist faces danger or crisis often embodied in other characters. As the player struggles against antagonists (and sometimes themselves), their relationship to the concept of control provides the conduit for our empathy, and by extension, how we engage the story’s themes.

Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000).

Ghost in the Shell (1995).











Genshin Impact (2020).

God of War (2018).
We feel empathy towards protagonists. This dynamic operates as a cycle found in popular literature and Hollywood films: we get to know our character’s internal reality by seeing the choices they make under stress.

Final Fantasy VII Remake (2020).

The Last of Us Part II (2020).










Once we understand what they want, we anticipate what they might do, and we also witness good and bad things happening to them.
Therefore, the story is composed of a range of strong and mild surprises.
The cycle repeats with different or progressed dilemmas.

Bones and All (2022).










Sometimes the character must discover their internal reality in order to control their external one.

The Matrix (1999).











Sound of Metal (2019).
Other times, after they fail to control their external world, they discover insight: perhaps they learn that they were not struggling against others, but against themselves.











Baba Is You (2019).
No doubt, Game Design includes providing players the experiences of discovery and control.










But narrative games complicate the protagonist paradigm.
In such video games, there are two main characters: the protagonist and the player.
The narrative films we watch center on their protagonist. The narrative games we study can have a protagonist too (the player character), but they also make room for another main character: the player, and the story created by what the player does.
This is why our early assignments isolate four player roles, framing storytelling through what the player can and does do.










The Investigator

Tacoma (2017).
Assignment 1: The Investigator










The Investigator

Firewatch (2016).

The Investigator role embraces much of what we know from the detective and mystery genres of literature and cinema.
The character searches for clues and engages other characters to discover the story.
The game’s plot is the player’s attempt at gathering information, and the story is the resulting sequence of events we mentally, and retrospectively, stitch together in our minds.

L.A. Noire (2011).

Chinatown (1974).










The Investigator role provides an excellent framework for environmental storytelling.











Dark Souls III (2016), Firelink Shrine — facing the five thrones of the Lords of Cinder.
Dark Souls III is not focused on The Investigator, but it repeatedly creates Investigator experiences. The player reads item descriptions and messages, inspects objects, listens to NPCs, and studies architecture and remains to reconstruct what happened.
The environmental designer embeds clues, events, and characters in the world. They are part level designer, architect, and teller of tales.











*Installation at The Broad, Los Angeles
The Investigator
We find such storytelling in a myriad of forms, including themed entertainment (such as Disneyland), escape rooms, alternate reality games, and museums.










The Investigator

Global Conflicts: Palestine.
Because The Investigator primarily discovers (rather than controls), this role provides straightforward mechanics for real-world topics.











Her Story (2015) — a story discovered in the past tense.
Games featuring the other three roles tell their stories in the present tense.
But The Investigator discovers the story that happened in the past.










Plot and story
Detective fiction gives us the cleanest version of this distinction, and it is worth naming precisely.

The plot is the order in which the player encounters the investigation.
The story is the underlying sequence of events, assembled retrospectively.

Chinatown and The Maltese Falcon both work this way. The detective changes very little in the world. The clues, the motives, and the relationships are all in place before the film begins — what changes over the course of it is comprehension.
Designing for The Investigator means designing the plot: deciding what the player finds, and in what order, so that the story assembles itself in their head.










What visual techniques might be handy for your Investigator project?
How about mechanics?

reads, looks, finds, collects











The Traveler

Everything (2017).
Assignment 2: The Traveler











Twin Peaks: The Return (2017) — the Red Room as a labyrinth to be navigated.
The Traveler
The Traveler explores in order to discover situations and events.
Often, they navigate labyrinths.











Zork.
The Traveler’s power is to find their path and to bear witness to the story.











The Unfinished Swan (2012).
That path can be narrative or spatial (or both).











A Short Hike (2019).
The Traveler’s journey ponders free will.










Maze and Labyrinth
We use these two words in a specific way:

A maze is what the word normally evokes — a puzzle of pathways, designed to be solved.
A labyrinth is a maze plus meaning. It is architecture built to carry a story or a metaphor.

The Traveler moves through a labyrinth, not a maze. The difference is whether the space is something to solve or something to undergo.
Umberto Eco separates mazes by how they branch:

Unicursal — one winding path, no choices. You cannot get lost, because there is only one route.
Multicursal — branches, dead ends, and decisions at every intersection.
Network — every point can connect to many others. No fixed start, no fixed end.











What visual techniques might be handy for your Traveler project?
How about mechanics?

walks, chooses, sees, explores











The Entrant
Situated Player Role 3: The Entrant
The Entrant has arrived at a boundary.
Unlike The Traveler, who moves through space as an interpretive act, The Entrant confronts a blocked passage. Progress is possible — but only by satisfying conditions.
The player asks: How does this world work?











Uncharted.
The Entrant reads what is present, tests what the system accepts or rejects, and gradually learns the rules governing passage.
The threshold might be a locked door, a puzzle room, a boss, a border, or a bureaucratic procedure.











Portal (2007) — the chamber itself is a spatial threshold.
In Portal, passage is not blocked by a conventional locked door. The player must reorganize space by creating a non-Euclidean pathway through the chamber.
The player does not merely find the path, as The Traveler might. They must understand and manipulate the room’s system to make passage possible.











Papers, Please (2013) — a bureaucratic threshold.
Not every threshold is architectural. In Papers, Please, the player becomes the threshold: inspecting documents, applying changing rules, and deciding who may cross the border.
The act of accepting or rejecting passage becomes the story.










The Shift to Control
The Entrant marks the framework’s major shift from discovery toward control.
Agency is no longer expressed merely through movement or interpretation, but by demonstrating alignment with the system’s demands.










The Entrant’s loop: L.O.P.
The puzzle-platformer Inside (2016) consistently manifests a repeatable three-step loop: Legibility, Opportunity, and Performance.

Inside (2016) — Legibility.
Legibility: See what matters. The player recognizes the barrier and identifies the interactive components in the room.











Inside (2016) — Opportunity.
Opportunity: Imagine the solution. By experimenting with individual mechanics, the player imagines how the components might be configured or sequenced.











Inside (2016) — Performance.
Performance: Test the idea. The player attempts to carry out the imagined solution. The system accepts or rejects the performance.
The Investigator learns what happened. The Traveler reaches the boundary. The Entrant tests whether understanding and action are sufficient to cross it.
The threshold does more than halt progress: it defines the player’s relationship to the world and its rules.










What visual techniques make a threshold legible?
How do the mechanics let the player imagine and perform a solution?

reads, tests, configures, performs











The Dreamer

John Tenniel’s illustration for Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865).
Assignment 3: The Dreamer











Humanity (2023).

Inception (2010).
The Dreamer

Inside (2016).
The Dreamer strives to control their environment, but unlike The Entrant — who confronts a material reality — The Dreamer confronts a symbolic one.
The world expresses an internal state, and the player must interpret that expression in order to act.
The player asks: What does this world express?

Baba Is You (2019).

Braid (2008).











The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920).
With this role, the world is rich and vibrant.
Like in expressionistic cinema from early 20th century, the world holds the intrigue.











The Witness (2016).
At the level of mechanics, a Dreamer game may resemble an Entrant game: both can use puzzles.
The distinction is not whether the player solves a puzzle, but whether the puzzle also functions as metaphor.











Alice in Wonderland (Disney, 1951).
Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland provides an excellent entry point for the shift between The Entrant and The Dreamer.
The Entrant approach: Alice tries a key in a locked door. The problem follows grounded logic, but she is too large to pass through.
The Dreamer approach: she must drink from a bottle and eat cake, changing her body and accepting the dream logic of the world.
The Entrant’s threshold demands mastery of how the world works. The Dreamer’s threshold demands recognition of what the world expresses.











Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022).
_We take on the same task as our character –
interpreting images in order to take the next steps. 

_Such images are both symbolic and a piece of the puzzle.











Papo & Yo (2012).
The task of interpreting what the thing can do…
How is that connected to interpreting what it means?











Humanity (2023).
But it is not only the puzzle pieces that are symbolic, but (like with our own dreams), the overall experience is worth interpreting.











Paprika (2006) — a world that is explicitly an externalized dream.
In some cases, the worlds are not merely dream-like but are explicitly externalized dreams. 











Inside (2016).
We might not have access to The Dreamer’s thoughts in the way we expect from a traditional protagonist.
In this case, the player character is like a blank canvas for what we are thinking, therefore the avatar’s visual rendering might lack detail.










The Alice Shift
Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland shows the exact moment The Entrant becomes The Dreamer. Alice is stuck in a hallway, behind a locked door only ten inches high.

The Entrant approach — rationality. She tries the key in the locks. It fits the small door, but she cannot fit through it. She reasons about keys and doors as material things.
The Dreamer approach — surrealism. She goes back to the table and finds a bottle labeled “DRINK ME.” To get through, she has to accept the logic the world is offering and change her own body to match it.

The Entrant’s threshold asks the player to master how the world works. The Dreamer’s threshold asks them to recognize what the world is expressing.
The L.O.P. loop still runs here — but legibility becomes the hard part rather than the first step. In Papo & Yo, the puzzles are a metaphor for living with an alcoholic parent. The player still solves them; the meaning is in what solving them reveals. The mechanics are the language.










What visual techniques might be handy for your Dreamer project?
How about mechanics?

Instructor notesinterprets, connects, transforms, configures











Roles Overlap

Death Stranding (2019).
HOLD ON!
Most games – especially AAA games – oscillate among roles.
Players Can
investigate, travel, cross thresholds, solve, and interpret










How would you describe other playable roles?
In…
Procedural Narrative
(Tabletop) Role Playing Games (both the DM and the players)
*What else?
_*This is your challenge going forward. To become a games scholar _.

534/Lectures/Week-2.1---The-Value-of-Unc.content:
Three topics we’ll be juggling for Project 1

Investigator, Protagonist, Visual Grammar











Sources
The Value of Uncertainty
Four Authors – philosophers and psychologist
aeon.co/essays/use-uncertainty-to-leverage-the-power-of-your-predictive-brain










keywords
Certainty, uncertainty, volatility, surprise, explore, information, solution, control










Three Stages
3 Stages


Expected Uncertainty


Unexpected Uncertainty


Volatility












Concepts
First, let’s focus on some concepts.










Mental Model


What a person believes or thinks they know about a system


A person’s expectations of an external reality, a simplified version


Constructed from their past experiences













A retail site interrupts the visit with an email-capture pop-up.

A newsletter page and its navigation rail.
Because of the pop up, clicking the back button takes them back to google, the actual first page.










Predictive Processing
Human brains are designed to minimize their own average surprise (prediction error) during
real-life exchanges with the world.










Predictive Processing: Peter’s Preemptive Summary
When we find ourselves at a prediction level at “medium” as opposed to “excellent” or “terrible”, we respond by seeking more information for our model – compelling us to be open to learning and exploring.
This can be fun. (Careful with that word, “fun”).


                  
                  Instructor shares 
                  
                

This is Peter’s interpretation and take. Including coupling learning with fun.












We probe the world in ways that aim to reveal just where the key uncertainties lie, so that by future actions they can resolve them and move on.
We seek new information and engage in complex rituals such as art…whose role is to safely reveal and stress-test our own deepest assumptions.










epistemic (knowledge-seeking) ----- discovery
pragmatic (puzzle-solving) ----------- control










1. Expected Uncertainty
Expected uncertainty is experienced whenever we know the weak spots in our information, and we can take action accordingly (i.e. control).
We are equipped to ‘think things through’ in advance of acting because we have a workable mental model.










An example: registration
You want to enroll in a popular class that has 2 sections, but maybe 3.


The 8am (Bad) — T/Th. Undesirable time. Fills last, but it does fill.


The Monday night (Ok) — 6–9pm, one three-hour block. This is adequate.


The rumored Wednesday noon (Great) — drops between your two other classes. No extra trip to campus. Ideal.












The night before
You don’t know how fast the Monday (the OK one) night fills.
But you know the 8am (Bad) goes last. You know roughly how last year went. You wonder if the noon section (Great) is only a rumor.
You don’t know what will happen, but you know exactly where your ignorance is.










The plan is clean
Running “if I take the Monday night (OK), I still have a seat, and I can watch for noon (Great)” in your head, before touching the portal.
→ Thinking is an action. It harvests information from the model you already have.
And the plan is correct. Switching is free and easy, so grabbing a fallback costs you nothing. You end up with a seat either way, and the noon section stays in reach.










Precision
“We were told a third might open” — by whom?
A department admin’s email and a group-chat rumor are the same information at different confidence.
The confidence decides how much of the plan you build around it.










2. Unexpected Uncertainty
Unexpected uncertainty typically occurs when the environment (the rule structure) changes without our being in a position to predict that change.
This might be my cue to move into exploratory mode.
Predictive brains expect control and, if it fails, they drive learning.
We know there is a pattern. We just have to discover it.










The rule changes
You take the Monday night.  And it fills.
Then the registrar posts a new drop/add rule — you have to drop a class before you can add another.  There is not longer a ‘swapping’ option.
You know from past experience that dropping takes the system 5 to 30 minutes to complete.
Your plan wasn’t wrong. It was made under different rules.










Now it’s a dilemma
Explore vs. exploit. There was no tradeoff yesterday, because enrolling was free. This new delay in changing sections - a period of minutes in which you are enrolled in nothing -  manufactures one.










What you do next
Email the advisor. Ask people who registered yesterday whether the lock hit them. Check whether it applies to waitlist auto-enrolls.
That’s the learning rate going up.  You attempt discovery.
The registrar has rules. They’re just not published.










3. Volatility
Volatility is subtly different: it names a situation in which the frequency of changes in the rules or situation are themselves rapidly changing.
Uncertainty about the uncertainty.










Registration, continued
Wednesday, the noon (Great) section is added. Just before you drop your OK section, the Great section is pulled.  Phew.
Thursday it’s back with a cap of 10 students.
Friday there’s a rumor of another one.










You can’t learn a rate
There’s no strategy to form, because the thing you’d form it about won’t hold still.
Uncertainty about the uncertainty.
You either freeze — stay in the Monday night (Ok), stop checking, let the noon section go —
or refresh the portal every ten minutes for four days and learn nothing.
That’s the tell: your choices stopped paying. What’s left is only how you cope with that.










Volatility
With unexpected uncertainty (#2), our strategies can work – in our mode of learning and openness.
But with volatility, our strategies are suspect. People and animals find this situation extremely uncomfortable.










We recognize that our ability to discover is weak, therefore we have no control.










Marvel Snap
The same three stages, in a game










Marvel Snap — Expected Uncertainty

Marvel Snap (2022) — the collection screen.
The Player,
“I don’t know exactly what is going to happen. But I am quite oriented.”










Marvel Snap — Unexpected Uncertainty

Marvel Snap (2022) — building a deck.

*Marvel Snap
A new ability - a card whose On Reveal ability changes the location itself.*










Marvel Snap — Volatility
Our cards are taken away
and we are forced into
a “Redemption Round”


                  
                  Instructor notes 
                  
                

I made this up. I don’t know if I’m playing AI, if this round will win my cards back or if there’s no connection.
There’s no example in Marvel Snap because volatility is bad, so you’re not going to see it in a game like this.












Art
Art has expected uncertainty (#1),
and unexpected uncertainty (#2).
Our predictive models are encountered as objects →
we understand our own expectations.










This reveal can be a way of materializing and confronting our own high-level assumptions, about self, world and other, but doing so in a framework that steps back from daily concerns.











Certain and uncertain, against pretend (practice) and real.

Course Description
Is Life A Story or a Game?
We will study and practice how narrative video games express meaning, make topics and themes playable, and how they uniquely invoke the player’s emotions.
Artists want to communicate in order to question and persuade. What does this mean for narrative game design?
This course has four overarching topics.

Visual Grammar
Storytelling: The Player Character’s Role and Situation
Worldbuilding: Playable Worlds Expressive Through The Space’s Edges
Pragmatic Practices for Creators

The first two topics focus on two principles at a narrative designer’s disposal: the language of the moving image and the video game player’s role. The third considers the game world itself: how its limits, rules, and responses can express meaning through play.
The fourth topic — pragmatic creative practices — explores how successful artists imagine compelling ideas, execute on a small scale, and participate in a culture of critique and creative growth.
Grammar
We study the visual grammar of cinema and how it provides a valuable starting point for how video games tell stories. We consider how color, lighting, composition, montage, and cinematography shape our attention in order to communicate.
Cinema language is also sonic. Audio design represents one of the most powerful and flexible of the narrative game designer’s tools, and film audio shows us much of what is possible in video games.
Playable Roles
Mainstream storytelling features a character who attempts to control their reality. They want something, and we anticipate how they might get it. What comes next: surprises. Some surprises are small, some are large.
With this canon in hand, we continue with mainstream alternatives, such as stories that do not conclude with the protagonist attaining power, but instead, stories that close with an emphasis on the character (and player) discovering insight and understanding.
Further, all narrative games complicate the protagonist paradigm as there are two main characters: the protagonist and the player.
In summary, we study how narrative game situations inform what the player can and does do.
Worldbuilding
Situations also provide our way into worldbuilding. As the player moves from one situation to the next, they meet the world, learn its rules, experience its responses, and discover what lies at or beyond its edges.
Rather than treating a world as setting or backstory—or pursuing size and exhaustive lore—we focus on making playable worlds feel coherent, inhabited, and expressive through their limits.
Creative Practices
Throughout the semester we will learn pragmatic creative practices. How do successful artists imagine and articulate their nascent ideas? What techniques maximize the goal of tackling compelling projects that student teams can reasonably create?
The ultimate outcome of this course is to prepare you for subsequent classes in which you will be expected to quickly imagine compelling game ideas and then make them.

A Perspective
Stories embody two apparently conflicting impulses — to connect us to something real at the same time inviting us to believe in magic. The novelist Marcel Theroux frames the paradox of stories this way. He says that storytelling wobbles between authenticity and enchantment. On one hand, we want stories to feel like they must be real for someone, and on the other, we want to engage the possibility of what cannot exist.

All lectures and discussions are for the sake of shaping and inspiring the course’s assignments.

Another Perspective
Insert the word “story” in the place of “book” and consider what’s happening today. From David Bell: “It is here, with this question of engagement, that the comparison between the Enlightenment and A.I.’s supposed ‘second Enlightenment’ breaks down and reveals something important about the latter’s limits and dangers. When readers interact imaginatively with a book, they are still following the book’s lead, attempting to answer the book’s questions, responding to the book’s challenges and therefore putting their own convictions at risk.”

Learning Objectives
Visual and Interactive Storytelling

Describe how visual storytelling approaches build subtext and theme with an emphasis on point-of-view.
Understand color theory and lighting in order to compose communicative visual designs.
Create story stakes, pressure, and growth for your characters.
Compare how cinematic and interactive storytelling techniques express change and contrast. For example, evaluate how video editing creates montage in order to understand relevant approaches in game language.
Analyze the arc of experience in films and games.
Discuss how prior art research inspires your work.

Digital Media Development

Construct interactive worlds in the Unity game engine (literacy).
Translate photography and video camera operation to game camera principles.
Understand the essential components of 3D models, including materials, textures, and meshes, in order to incorporate them in-game.
Create rich and meaningful sound designs.

Production Methods

Explain how self-direction couples with shared creative visions.
Give and take critique.
Use ideation, brainstorming, and prototyping approaches.

Readings
There are many more readings in the class folder than any student will be asked to read.

Painting with Light by John Alton
The Science of Storytelling by Will Storr

Library of Babel by Luis Borges

Attendance and Punctuality
Students receive one forgiven absence over the semester. Beginning with the second absence, each additional absence lowers the final course grade by 3 points. For example, a final grade of 100 becomes 97.
Four late arrivals, accumulated across the semester, count as one absence. That absence is included in the same forgiveness and subsequent deductions.
If Peter is ever late to class, attendance will not be taken that day. In addition, every student receives one additional forgiven absence to use later in the semester.
This attendance adjustment is applied after all other course-grade calculations and accumulates with additional absences.
Grading: Assignment Deadlines
Assignments are due at the scheduled class time unless their assignment page states otherwise. There are no forgiven late or missing assignments.
For each of the three projects:

A project submitted within 24 hours after its due class time lowers the final course grade by 5 points.
A project submitted more than 24 hours after its due class time, or never submitted, lowers the final course grade by 10 points.

For each milestone (for the projects), a submission after its due class time—or no submission—lowers the final course grade by 2 points, whether it is submitted within 24 hours or later.
These deductions accumulate and are applied after all other course-grade calculations.

AI/index.title: Queryable Knowledge Bases
AI/index.content:
Here for PB Office Hours — the game design guide itself? Go straight there →

Here to learn about and make a queryable knowledge base?
A queryable knowledge base is a folder of plain text files on your own computer that you can ask questions of — your course material, your research, your production notes, your team’s scattered documents, gathered in one place and written so an AI can read all of it. Point any AI at it and it takes on a particular expertise you’ve crafted, for your own use or anyone else’s.
Why this and not browser chat
When you use ChatGPT or Claude in a browser tab, you rebuild context every time. You paste in the document, explain the project again, remind it what you decided last week. The conversation is where the work lives, and returning to a chat days later can be confusing, they are hard to share, and impossible to version.
A knowledge base remedies that. The work lives files you can read and write when you like. The AI is a collaborator you invite in. Walk away from the session, come back in a month, hand the same folder to a colleague.
The practical difference is that you stop managing chats and start growing an asset.
Peter’s guiding question through all of this: when I use AI, am I thinking more or less?

The fundamentals
Six ideas.
Markdown — plain text files ending in .md, with a couple of formatting conventions for headings and links. Readable in any text editor, on any machine.
A persistent workspace — a folder on disk that both you and an AI return to. “Workspace” already means something to those of us who use Unity or Unreal: a local project, persistent across sessions and collaborators. Same idea, applied to documents instead of code/game assets.
Command line interface, CLI — an AI tool that works inside a folder. It reads your files, writes new ones, moves things around, and checks its own work. Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity are the current ones.
Each of these ships two ways. The terminal version is the original and raw version.  The GUI/desktop version is a polished window built on the same underlying agent, with more features: a chat-style interface, buttons to approve or reject what it wants to do, file previews, and so on.
In-context learning — the AI learns from what you place in front of it, live, in the moment — the files it’s currently holding in memory for this session. Think of when using chat, you give it a sentence or two (of context) before asking your question. But with ICL, you can provide 100 sentences. Or 100,000. In practice this shows up a few ways: pasting in a style guide so it writes like you instead of generically; handing it a few examples of the thing you want (“here are three good ones, now do a fourth”) instead of describing the rules; giving it a whole codebase, or a whole knowledge base, so it answers from your actual material instead of guessing; or writing down your own standing instructions in a file it reads every time, so you’re not re-explaining your preferences in every conversation.
Context engineering — the craft of arranging files so an AI finds what matters without being told every time: which files load, in what order, within what budget. Indexes, naming, a note at the root that explains the folder. This is the actual skill, and it is more editorial than technical.
Obsidian — a free text editor for markdown files. It shows your folder and file structure in a sidebar, the way VS Code does for a codebase. A “vault” is just a folder.
Two more you will meet later: Git and GitHub, which make a knowledge base versioned and shareable, and frontmatter, options for labels markdown files for searching and organizing.
How this looks together
Imagine Sophie, a history grad student.  She has three years of archive notes as .docx files with names like notes2.docx. She converts them to markdown, tags each by decade and topic in its frontmatter, and opens the folder in Obsidian to read and write them.  As unit, all these markdown files are called a vault.  When she points a coding agent’s desktop app at that same folder, it becomes a persistent workspace she returns to across writing sessions. When she asks “what have I found on wartime rationing?”, in-context learning means it reads her files and answers from them. It finds the right three notes out of three hundred because she previously did some context engineering: folders named by decade, files named for what’s in them, and a short index note at the root of each folder listing what’s inside and why.

Here’s how — 20-30 minutes, hands on
The fastest way to understand all of the above is to do it once on someone else’s mess.
In a moment, you will download a fictional two-person student team’s terribly disorganized project folder, with three conflicting schedules, contradictory notes, and file names like GDD_v2_FINAL_deloris-comments.md. You point an AI at it and reorganize it into a working vault.
You are learning three things at once: how a coding agent behaves, what a persistent workspace is, and what context engineering does.
→ Your First Persistent Workspace
A note on tools. That tutorial uses Codex, because USC provides it to faculty and students. (A “Plus” subscription is $20 a month otherwise).  The lesson transfers to any LLM.  For example, Gemini’s free tier can do this, and the various Chinese models are inexpensive.  Claude’s and Codex’s free tiers cannot engage this tutorial’s lesson.

Then point it at your own material
The next pass is your own folder — a course you teach, a research area, a project’s documents. Copy it first, work on the copy.
The prompts that do most of the work are unglamorous:

Read through all of this and orient me to it. Don’t give advice on the merits.
Suggest how to organize this. Move, create, edit, and archive whatever helps. Consider context engineering practices such as indexes. Archive anything made obsolete rather than deleting it.
What would you need to read to answer a question about this now, compared to before?

Use your tool’s plan mode if it has one — it proposes what it intends to do before doing it.

A worked example, if you want one
Peter carried this a long way for his own courses: PB Office Hours is an accumulated teaching material — tutorials, a reference wiki, storytelling frameworks — arranged so an AI becomes a guide for students to talk to.
PBOH is a narrow example of what is possible.   But it does show what a knowledge base becomes after months of tending, and the whole thing is public if you want to read the insides.
If you want to see one running before building your own, the quick starts each take you from nothing installed to a first conversation, one page per tool.

Background

Keep Your AI Where I Can See It — the talk this page came out of. Built to be spoken over, so it reads sparse; the appendices at the end have the practical detail on accounts, models, and costs.
Andrej Karpathy’s LLM wiki — the same idea, arrived at independently.
Google’s Open Knowledge Format — a recent attempt to standardize what a folder like this should look like.

geidai/index.title: Worldbuilding Intensive
geidai/index.content:
Tokyo University of the Arts (Geidai) · July 7–10, 2026
Instructor: Peter Brinson, Professor of Practice, University of Southern California
Through lectures, exercises, and workshops, students explore worldbuilding as a foundation for game design and development. The intensive uses a design framework called  Bounded Worlds, which encourages students to build small playable worlds that are expressive through their limits.

Worldbuilding, Bounded
Every game design project faces the same challenge: our initial ideas are too large to build. The Bounded Worlds framework is a direct response. It encourages worlds that are expressive through their limits.
Because the world has overt limits, the designer can focus on a manageable set of situations. Brian Upton defines a situation as an interval of play that contains a choice. Even a small handful of situations can make a playable world vibrant and engaging. The player navigates a path through them; through exploration, choice becomes expressive within constraint.
By the end of the intensive, you will make a playable world — a bounded world.
The Three Boundarie Types
There are three ways a Bounded World can treat its edges — three Boundaries. Some feel complete in themselves. Some present edges that can be approached but not passed. Others are structured around boundaries the player can, and wants to, cross.
To decide which is yours, ask: does the world imply or provide an outside?
If it doesn’t, the world is Finite. If it does, ask whether the player can reach it — an outside implied but withheld is Closed; an edge the player passes through is a Threshold.

Finite — The world presents itself as whole. The player engages entirely within what is present; the accessible world is everything.
Closed — The player can encounter the edge of the world. The boundary is present and meaningful, but cannot be passed.
Threshold — The player approaches and passes from one state or space into another.

See Bounded Worlds for worked examples of each.
